text: Retained catalogue This page comes from the retained catalogue. Its launch instructions and native results describe the earlier tree, now preserved under rescued/part2 , rather than the current launcher. The documentation build does not rerun these examples. Thirteen original Apache-2.0 examples for FontLab 9. Each entry verifies a fixture SHA-256, copies its VFJ to a new temporary directory, opens that copy and closes exactly that package in finally . Copy paths are resolved before opening so macOS /var and /private/var refer to the same owned document. Successful cleanup removes the working directory; failed close retains it. Nothing saves over testdata. Font attribution and licences remain in the fixture manifest . All modules import outside FontLab. Entry functions need FontLab's fontlab , fontgate objects and fontpr bridge. The pen/export entries additionally need FontTools installed in FontLab's Python 3.11 interpreter. TypeRig and Fontport are not required for these thirteen scripts. Run edits in a dedicated no-document FontLab session through the workspace native runner. Native status: 13/13 passed on 2026-10-16, FontLab 9.0.9783 (workspace receipt: verification/issue-106/evidence/getgo/examples3-all/receipt.json ). The receipt covers run() , declared assertions, owned cleanup and unchanged fixtures; host-free tests remain separate.
title: Real GetGo fonts, disposable working copies

text: These are repository-checkout demos, not standalone Scripts-folder installations. Keep the checkout (including testdata/getgo ) together and put its root on sys.path once, then import an example: import sys sys . path . insert ( 0 , "/path/to/fontlab-python-examples" ) from examples.getgo import font_audit print ( font_audit . run ()) Each script also has a MenuTitle and prints its result when executed from the Scripting panel as __main__ ; keep that root on sys.path for this route too. No script chooses the current font. The UI returns an explicitly owned handle; all other results are dictionaries. Mutation entries enforce the no-document requirement before reading fixtures or creating a working directory and name any open documents in the error. Read-only examples may coexist with other fonts.
title: Repository-checkout demos: run inside FontLab

text: font_audit.py uses GG Baar (CC0-1.0). Measured: 96 glyphs, 95 encoded scalars, 2048 UPM, and no anchors. The report also covers vertical metrics, unencoded names and Unicode collisions. GG Baar has zero anchors: both counts make that explicit, alongside missing A/H top anchors. The explicit anchor policy demonstrates a check; an absent anchor is not automatically a font defect.
title: font_audit — metrics, encoding and anchor policy (native passed; 0.21 s)

text: unicode_coverage.py uses Zoto Kufi Arabic (Apache-2.0). run(text="مرحبا بالعالم 123") compares native encodings against unique scalars through a Unicode-only reader. Measured: eight covered code points; U+0031/U+0032/U+0033 are missing. U+0627 is covered; no layer/anchor lookup is needed. Encoding coverage does not prove contextual shaping.
title: unicode_coverage — Arabic sample text (native passed; 0.27 s)

text: outline_pens.py uses GG Hint (Apache-2.0). A/B/O contours pass through FontTools BoundsPen/AreaPen for exact curve bounds and signed areas. Measured A/B/O: 2/3/2 contours, 11/55/42 points; winding labels and FontLab hasIntersPoints boundary-intersection index pairs. Contained counters and self-intersections are outside the pairwise test; this is not filled-region boolean overlap detection or overlap removal. Each native recording converts QPointF operands to tuples before segment-pen validation; open paths require endPath , closed paths closePath . This receipt validates closed native contours; native open-path coverage remains a follow-up.
title: outline_pens — bounds, direction and complexity (native passed; 0.18 s)

text: naming.py uses GG Baar (CC0-1.0). Measured: assigned family, style, preferred and PostScript names read back; family becomes Scripting Sample , PS name ScriptingSample-Regular . Copyright/licence stay intact. The small policy accepts ASCII letters, digits and spaces and enforces the 63-character PS limit. Changes are discarded on close.
title: naming — name a disposable derivative (native passed; 0.12 s)

text: kerning_classes.py uses GG Stroke Chan OFL Italic (OFL-1.1). Measured on the Italic master: default-master pair count, typed pair sides, explicit zero values, class members/modes and dangling member names. The default run(limit=5) returns totals (619 pairs across 79 left sides, 233 classes) and up to five pairs, classes and members per class; run(limit=None) returns complete data. Opaque native modes become text for JSON. No class expansion or OFL font renaming occurs.
title: kerning_classes — pairs retain their meaning (native passed; 0.19 s)

text: designspace.py uses GG Cosm (CC0-1.0). Measured: three masters, one wght axis, separate user/design ranges, master and eight export-instance coordinates in axis order. valueWeight reads design coordinates. The selected master stays unchanged; no interpolation is implied.
title: designspace — axes, masters and instances (native passed; 0.26 s)

text: master_compatibility.py uses GG Plum (CC0-1.0). Measured: A/V/a match across all three masters; reports include closed flags, compatible and missing_layers . Missing layers differ from empty layers. Equal topology does not prove component compatibility, contour correspondence or interpolation quality.
title: master_compatibility — compare direct-contour topology (native passed; 0.23 s)

text: spacing.py uses GG Baar (CC0-1.0). It plans I's shift/new width, moves direct nodes and anchors and reads bearings back. Measured: I's bearings [128, 0], shift 48, new width 416, plus plan and resulting sidebearings . The fixed H/I inputs have direct outlines; only I on the owned font's default master changes. The basic node/anchor move follows the existing sidebearing recipe ; this demo adds an owned real input, an RSB-aware plan and bounds from re-read nodes of the straight-line I outline; native cached boundingBox/contourRect remain stale.
title: spacing — I borrows H's bearings (native passed; 0.11 s)

text: batch_transform.py uses GG Baar (CC0-1.0). run(scale=1.1) preflights both glyphs and scales direct node/anchor x coordinates and advances, retaining y coordinates. Expected: A/V point counts Measured A/V widths: 640 → 704. Readback re-fetches the layer and contours instead of inspecting the wrappers just assigned; anchors and advance widths are checked too. Scaling about x=0 also scales both sidebearings. Only the disposable default master changes; source data stays intact.
title: batch_transform — widen A and V (native passed; 0.11 s)

text: export_ttf.py uses GG Baar (CC0-1.0). Native contour pens capture .notdef , space , A , V ; the font closes before Cu2QuPen/TTGlyphPen and FontBuilder create a TTF geometry subset. The native pen adapter detaches QPointF coordinates into ordinary tuples for both exports. Measured: verified: true , format: glyf , retained binary path, exact glyph order/cmap/advances/UPM and full licence name record. Reopened bounds must agree within two units for curve conversion and coordinate rounding. Every contour is also measured with AreaPen after binary reopening: TTF signs must reverse the source signs, and CFF signs must match. winding_verified and per-contour winding reports expose those checks without assuming absolute source winding.
title: export_ttf — compile and reopen quadratic outlines (native passed; 0.17 s)

text: export_otf.py uses GG Baar (CC0-1.0). T2CharStringPen builds the same subset as CFF OpenType. Measured: verified: true , format: CFF and the same readback checks. Both exports accept run(destination="/absolute/new-sample.otf") (use .ttf for TTF); the default retains a new temporary export directory. Existing files and symlinks are refused. Outputs are named Scripting Sample , with complete CC0 text, copyright and public source URL. These geometry subsets omit native hints, features, kerning, axes and other layers. They demonstrate pen interchange, not FontLab's export profiles.
title: export_otf — compile and reopen CFF outlines (native passed; 0.11 s)

text: font_info_ui.py uses GG Stroke Chan OFL Italic (OFL-1.1). It closes the font before showing a QtGui QDialog with a plain text QLabel. Measured: GG Stroke Chan OFL, 106 glyphs, 1000 UPM, Italic master. Retain the handle: tool = font_info_ui.run() , inspect tool.report / tool.widget , call tool.close() in finally , then drain deferred deletion events in the native runner. The Scripting-panel __main__ route calls canonical-module show() , which retains font_info_ui.TOOL even when panel globals are discarded; a second launch closes the predecessor. Native acceptance must exercise this route and verify the plain-text enum, visibility and deferred deletion. Cleanup is idempotent. No signals, QApplication or second loop are created.
title: font_info_ui — a tiny PythonQt tool (native passed; 0.15 s)

text: compare_fonts.py uses GG Baar (CC0-1.0) and GG Hint (Apache-2.0). Measured: 96 common glyphs, 274 Hint-only glyphs, none Baar-only; width differences in em units (right minus left), using each font's own UPM. Nested owned contexts close both documents even if opening or inspecting the second fails.
title: compare_fonts — compare in em units (native passed; 0.31 s)

text: native_manifest.json lists all entries, fonts, dependencies, observable checks, cleanup and measured native passes from the linked receipt. PYTEST_DISABLE_PLUGIN_AUTOLOAD = 1 uv run --no-project --with pytest python -m pytest -q tests FontLab's run_python has a fixed 5-second deadline . Never execute a complete run() synchronously through it: file opening, import cold starts and compilation can exceed it. Use the Scripting panel or an event-loop callback outside the request, keeping run_python calls to short setup/enqueue/poll operations. Preserve a detached result/error receipt and poll it; a client timeout is not a native pass. Manifest expected entries are machine assertions ( path plus exactly one of equals , len , contains , gt ), executed by _checks.assert_expected(result, row["expected"]) . Paths include dictionary keys, list indices and UI handle attributes. UI cleanup is explicitly handle.close . The manifest's native_followups retain save-prompt, metadata-renormalization, refreshed-bounds, segment-pen and Scripting-panel UI checks for the native worker. Add --with fonttools to uv run and target tests/test_getgo_scripts.py for real pens, binary and winding-tamper checks. No Fontport dependency or legacy scripts.py API remains; the needed master-report helper now lives in designspace.py.
title: Native execution and host-free verification

text: Retained catalogue This page comes from the retained catalogue. Its launch instructions and native results describe the earlier tree, now preserved under rescued/part2 , rather than the current launcher. The documentation build does not rerun these examples. 106 single-file PythonQt dialogs for everyday font work: anchors, metrics, kerning, outlines, masters, names, guides, font info, features, hinting, cleanup, generators, reports and proofs. Each one works on the current font and offers a master scope where that makes sense; most list what an Apply will change before you press it, and a few (such as mark-colour swatches) apply on click. Report, browser and proof scripts change no font data (some select glyphs, copy to the clipboard or export files). Many glyph-editing tools group their edits into one Undo step, but Undo coverage varies. Seven metrics scripts warn that moved stem hints are not restored, and font-wide data (font info, OpenType features, master settings) is written directly: Italic Angle (Masters) states that Undo does not restore its change. Read each script's notes before applying changes. Copy any file into FontLab's Scripts folder (for example Scripts/Samples ) and run it from the Scripts menu, or open it in the Scripting panel. A script needs only FontLab 9 and its bundled PythonQt; nothing else is installed. Dialogs are modeless, so the Font window stays usable, and every dialog disconnects its signals when closed. Each script was run in FontLab 9.0.9783 through its menu path on disposable copies of GetGo fonts, with screenshots and before/after reads of the changed glyphs. Edits on glyphs used by automatic composites warn first: FontLab may rebuild those composites' anchors and locks, and Undo does not restore that rebuild.
title: Samples: GUI scripts for FontLab 9

text: Script What it does Remove Empty Auxiliary Layers Delete empty auxiliary layers (no outlines, anchors, guides, note or other data) from the selected glyphs. Select Unreferenced Glyphs List unencoded glyphs that nothing references, and select them in the Font window for review.
title: Cleanup (2)

text: Script What it does Bump Font Version Bump the numeric version and version name; optionally append a dated font note. Calculate Vertical Metrics Set hhea, Win (and optionally OS/2 typo) vertical metrics to enclose every glyph, per master. Glyph Order Preview & Export Sort by Unicode, name or Unicode script; export one glyph name per line for the whole font. Master Metrics Table Edit ascender, descender, x-height and cap-height across masters; diagram follows the selected row. Names & Credits Edit family, style, credits and version naming for the current font. Unicode Ranges & Codepage Hints Report OS/2 range bits and complete printable codepage coverage from every glyph encoding; no font changes.
title: Font Info (6)

text: Script What it does Outline Effect Turn the selected glyphs into outlined (hollow) letters. Placeholder Glyphs Create empty placeholder glyphs from pasted glyph names or characters, on every master. Shadow Copy Add a shifted copy of the selected glyphs' outlines as a separate shadow element. Small Caps from Capitals Create small-cap glyphs (h.sc, a.sc ...) from the selected capitals, on every master. Superior & Inferior Figures Create superior (.sups) or inferior (.subs) copies of the selected figures, on every master. Tabular Figure Copies Create tabular (.tf) copies of the selected figures, on every master.
title: Generators (6)

text: Script What it does Clear Glyph Guides Remove glyph guides from the selected glyphs by direction and name. Copy Guides Between Masters Copy the glyph guides of one master to the other masters of the selected glyphs. Font Guides Panel Show the font's guides and add one named guide to every master of the selected glyphs. Grid Generator Add a regular grid of named glyph guides: N lines every S units from an origin. Guide List Editor Edit the glyph guides of one glyph as a table: X, Y, angle and name per master. Metric Reference Lines Add named horizontal glyph guides at the font's vertical metrics, plus an offset.
title: Guides (6)

text: Script What it does Autohint Selected Layers Run FontLab's PostScript autohinter on the selected glyphs, per master. Remove PostScript Hints Remove PostScript stem hints from the selected glyphs, horizontal and/or vertical, per master. Suggest Zones from Overshoots Set PostScript alignment zones from the overshoots of H/O (baseline, caps) and x/o (x-height).
title: Hinting (3)

text: Script What it does Classes Browser Browse kerning classes: their side, members, and every pair that uses them on each master. Compare Masters Line up every kerning pair across all masters and flag the ones that look inconsistent. Copy Between Masters Copy the kerning of one master to other masters, optionally scaled. Exceptions Finder Find kerning exceptions: pairs that override a class pair, and remove the ones you tick. Missing Pairs List the combinations of two glyph groups that no kerning pair covers on a master. Pair Editor Edit every kerning pair that involves one glyph, with one column per master. Pair List Browse every kerning pair of a master: filter, sort by any column, export to CSV. Pairs from Text Type a word, see each adjacent pair's kerning on every master, and set the ones you tick. Remove Small Pairs Delete kerning pairs whose value is smaller than a threshold, on one or all masters. Round Values Round kerning values to a step (5, 10 …) on one or all masters, previewing every change. Scale Values Scale all kerning values by a percentage on one or all masters. Text Preview Set text from the font's outlines with its kerning applied, per master, at any size.
title: Kerning (12)

text: Script What it does Back Up Master Layers Copy the master layers of the selected glyphs to named backup layers before risky edits. Compatibility Check Check that every master of each glyph can interpolate: same contours, nodes, anchors, components. Copy Layer Between Masters Copy the outline (and optionally anchors and advance width) from one master to others. Copy Outline to Mask Copy the outline of each selected glyph's master layer into its mask layer, for reference. Glyph Weight Chart Bar chart of the ink area of the selected glyphs in every master. Interpolation Preview Preview a glyph between two masters with a slider, from the masters' own nodes. Italic Angle Read and set the italic angle of every master, with a painted gauge comparing them. Layer Cleanup List the non-master layers of the selected glyphs (masks, backups, others) and delete the ticked ones. Master Switcher A small palette with one button per master: click to make that master current. Masters Overview One table of all masters: axis location, vertical metrics and italic angle. Restore Backup Layer Restore a backup layer (such as "Regular backup") into the master it was taken from. Sync Sidebearings Copy side-bearings from a reference master to the other masters, proportionally or as-is. Width Chart Line chart of the advance widths of the selected glyphs across masters.
title: Masters (13)

text: Script What it does Alignment Zones Edit the PostScript alignment zones (blue zones) of each master in a table. Centre in Advance Centre the outlines of the selected glyphs in their advance width, optionally with a new width. Copy from Reference Give the selected glyphs the sidebearings or the advance width of a reference glyph. Equalize Sidebearings Make the left and right sidebearings of the selected glyphs equal, on one or all masters. Italic Sidebearings Report and set sidebearings measured along the italic angle, not straight up. Round Advances Round advance widths to a step (2, 5, 10 … units), keeping every outline where it is. Scale Advances Scale the advance widths of the selected glyphs by a percentage, each outline staying centred. Sidebearings Tuner Set, add to or scale the side-bearings of the selected glyphs on one or all masters. Spacing String Preview Render a spacing control string such as HOHnono from the font's own outlines and advances. Tabular Width Give figures (and optionally currency signs) one shared advance width, each outline centred. Vertical Metrics Diagram See and edit ascender, cap height, x-height and descender of every master in one diagram. Width Table Advance widths of the selected glyphs across all masters, sortable, with odd progressions flagged. Zero-Width Marks Set the advance width of combining marks to zero, keeping or re-placing their outlines.
title: Metrics (13)

text: Script What it does Batch Rename Find and replace in glyph names (plain text or regular expression) with a live preview. Case Pairs Find the upper- or lowercase counterparts of the selected glyphs and select them. Character Info A live panel describing the character of the glyph selected in the Font window. Charset Compare Paste a text or a character set and compare it with the font's encoded characters. Duplicate Unicodes Find code points assigned to more than one glyph and remove them from the extra glyphs. Glyph Finder Type to find glyphs by name, character or code point; Enter selects them in the Font window. Glyph Notes Read and edit the note of the selected glyph, and browse every glyph that has a note. Glyph Tags View, add and remove glyph tags across the selected glyphs. Mark Color Palette Click a colour swatch to mark the selected glyphs with it (or clear the mark). Select by Mark Select glyphs in the Font window by their mark colour. Suffix Tool Add, remove or replace a glyph-name suffix (.ss01, .sc, .alt…) on the selected glyphs. Unicode from Names Assign Unicode code points derived from glyph names, with a preview first.
title: Names (12)

text: Script What it does Alternate Glyph Proof Compare a base glyph and its suffixed alternates in each master. Read-only; outlines share one scale per row. Feature Code Inspector Read-only feature source for the whole font. Choose a feature and search its code. Ligature Recipe Finder Find underscore-named glyphs and existing input glyphs. Name-derived recipes do not imply outline components. OpenType Class Browser Browse feature classes and their members. Filter by class name or glyph; font-wide across masters. Suffix Feature Report Suffix inventory across the whole font. Suggestions are naming hints; review the generated code. Suffix Substitution Builder Preview a font-wide suffix substitution. Append to source only; compile and test in the Features panel.
title: OpenType (6)

text: Script What it does Add Extremes Insert on-curve nodes at the horizontal and vertical extremes of curve segments. Contour Order View Show every master of a glyph side by side with numbered contours, start points and directions. Correct Contour Direction Set PostScript contour direction on the selected glyphs and report what changed per master. Delete Duplicate Contours Find contours drawn twice in the same layer and keep only the first copy. Delete Small Contours Remove contours whose area is below a threshold: stray specks left by drawing or tracing. Fix Zero Handles Find curve handles that sit on their own node and clean them up. Node Coordinates Panel A small live panel listing the selected nodes of the current glyph with coordinates. Node Statistics Contours and nodes per glyph and master in one table, with incompatible glyphs flagged. Optimize Start Points Move every contour's start node to its bottom-left on-curve node, consistently across masters. Remove Overlap Remove overlaps on the chosen masters of the selected glyphs, master compatibility checked first. Round Coordinates Round node coordinates of the selected glyphs to a grid, optionally anchors and component offsets. Slant Slant (skew) the selected glyphs by an angle, optionally the font's italic angle. Straighten Short Curves Turn short curve segments whose handles lie on the chord into straight lines. Transform Scale, skew, rotate and move the outlines of the selected glyphs with a live preview.
title: Outlines (14)

text: Script What it does Glyph Grid Show the selected glyphs on every master side by side, drawn from their outlines. Text by Master Render the same text once per master, stacked, to compare weight and width at a glance. Waterfall Render a line of text in a cascade of sizes, drawn straight from the glyph outlines. Small scripts for everyday glyph work, each tested in FontLab on a font it creates and throws away. text: Retained catalogue This page comes from the retained catalogue. Its launch instructions and native results describe the earlier tree, now preserved under rescued/part2 , rather than the current launcher. The documentation build does not rerun these examples. Purpose. Give every closed contour of the current master PostScript direction: outer contours counter-clockwise, counters clockwise (y-up). Nesting decides which is which, so a counter inside a counter turns outward again. Each contour then starts at its lowest, then leftmost on-curve node, which keeps start points compatible across masters. run () # all glyphs run ( glyph_names = [ "O" , "Q" ]) Orientation and nesting use the actual outline. Nesting is an exact ray-crossing test on the cubic and TrueType quadratic segments (recursive subdivision, not a fixed flattening), so a contour inside a curve's handles but outside the curve is an outer contour, and one hugging the inside of a curve is a counter. The recipe reads and plans every glyph before its first edit, so an unreadable glyph leaves the font unchanged. Collapsed contours (a single node, or all on-curve nodes at one point) have no direction: they are left alone and listed under skipped in the report. FontLab API. flContour.reverse() (keeps the first node, reverses the rest), flContour.setStartPoint(index) , flNode.isOn() . Orientation is computed from the node positions with the shoelace formula: in this FontLab 9 build flContour.clockwise reported False for a contour that runs clockwise in y-up coordinates, so the recipe doesn't rely on it. Native check ( native.py , owned font): an "O" drawn with both contours wrong ends with a counter-clockwise outer contour and a clockwise counter, both starting bottom-left, with the same points; a correct glyph is left alone. Provenance. The kind of task done by the clockwise/counter-clockwise and start-point (bottom-left) buttons of the TypeRig GUI Contour panel ( typerig-lib/Scripts/TypeRig GUI/Panel/Contour.py , MPL-2.0). text: The reference consumes Echopy's captured/enriched Python sources and adjacent stubs. It renders as the actual fontlab , fontgate , fontpr , PythonQt.* namespaces. Runtime inspection is disabled throughout normal documentation builds. Source checkout mode uses sibling ecosystem repositories. Installed artifact mode selects one provisioned Python package directory with FONTLAB_API_SOURCE_ROOT . Private sources are provisioned using authenticated GitHub tooling, without embedding credentials in the project. ./build.sh ./build.sh --check ./build.sh --serve The first environment synchronization may fetch locked dependencies. Once the dependency cache and source inputs exist, normal builds require neither FontLab nor network access. Explicit native refresh is a separate source-production operation; it captures inside FontLab before generation and enrichment. Generated coverage records every identity and exact source hash. Class indexes retain each member occurrence; identical captured text is linked to one full declaration. This sharing does not assert native inheritance or object identity. Before contributing, agree to the repository's FontLab contributor license agreement. Change source or enrichment inputs, regenerate, verify rendered references and cross-links, and include tests for changed behavior. Preserve source attribution and the Qt/PySide documentation licenses.

text: The source-lock helper compares documented inputs with their recorded SHA256 hashes. A normal build refuses changed input bytes. Review producer changes before requesting a lock refresh. Source-lock helper # this_file: scripts/source_lock.py """Pin the exact API source bytes across checkout and installed-artifact builds.""" import json from pathlib import Path def input_hashes ( inputs : list [ dict ]) -> dict [ str , str ]: """Reject duplicate input identities instead of silently dropping their bytes.""" actual = {} for row in inputs : if row [ "source" ] in actual : raise ValueError ( "Duplicate API source input: " + row [ "source" ]) actual [ row [ "source" ]] = row [ "sha256" ] return actual def verify_inputs ( locked : dict [ str , str ], inputs : list [ dict ]) -> None : """Fail for missing, new or modified source; never silently refresh a lock.""" actual = input_hashes ( inputs ) changed = sorted ( name for name in locked . keys () | actual . keys () if locked . get ( name ) != actual . get ( name ) ) if changed : raise ValueError ( "API source lock differs: " + ", " . join ( changed [: 10 ]) + "; use --update-source-lock after reviewing source changes." ) def apply_lock ( path : Path , inputs : list [ dict ], * , update : bool ) -> dict : """Write only when explicitly requested; ordinary builds verify the pin.""" sources = input_hashes ( inputs ) if update : path . write_text ( json . dumps ( { "schema_version" : 1 , "sources" : sources , }, indent = 2 , sort_keys = True , ) + " \n " ) if not path . exists (): raise FileNotFoundError ( "API source lock missing; use --update-source-lock." ) lock = json . loads ( path . read_text ()) verify_inputs ( lock [ "sources" ], inputs ) return lock

text: Use the reviewed wheel or source distribution from each package's GitHub release. Private repositories require authenticated access. Keep credentials in your normal GitHub tooling; never put them in documentation, URLs or Python scripts. Install outside FontLab with uv pip install PATH_TO_WHEEL . For embedded use, install into a Python directory on FontLab's interpreter path using a compatible Python version. FontLab supplies its native bindings and existing Qt application. The captured API uses FontLab9, Python3.11 and Qt5. The source-only documentation environment uses Python3.12 or newer. A PySide2 binary wheel is a reference input; it is not loaded into FontLab's PythonQt runtime. Enable FontLab's MCP server, then connect: from fontlab_remopy import FontLab with FontLab () as app : print ( app . fonts ()) print ( app . output ()) eval() returns a JSON-native value. run() captures stdout/stderr and a result; bind variables as keyword arguments rather than interpolating them into code. The native execution deadline still applies. A timeout can leave an operation's outcome unknown, so mutating calls are never retried automatically. with FontLab () as app : answer = app . eval ( "value + 2" , value = 40 ) execution = app . run ( "print(message) \n result = 42" , message = "Hello, FontLab" ) For asynchronous programs, use AsyncFontLab with async with and await calls.

text: Inside FontLab, echopy.fontlab delegates to the original fontlab objects; echopy.fontgate and echopy.fontpr follow the same contract. from echopy import fontlab as fl font = fl . CurrentFont () glyph = fl . CurrentGlyph () node = fl . flNode ( 120 , 340 ) Use flNode and the complete class member indexes to inspect captured signatures and enriched documentation. Any and variadic arguments mark incomplete native signature information. They are not permission to pass arbitrary objects; confirm an uncertain operation against the running host. title: Short imports

text: FontLab supplies PythonQt and an existing Qt5 application. Pythonqtside provides the QtCore/QtGui/QtWidgets namespace routing used by fly.qs . from pythonqtside import QtCore , QtWidgets The PySide2 reference package does not support the captured Python3.11 host. The expanded adapter will translate ordinary PySide2 app imports and binding behavior onto PythonQt, including property getters, constructors, signals, ownership, forms, models/views, painting, timers and processes. pythonqtside.run_app(path, *, parent=None) runs a PySide2 source file and its supported local imports inside FontLab's existing Qt application. It returns an AppHandle , retains execution globals, routes supported imports without replacing the host's import state, and tracks constructor-created Qt objects and connections for cleanup. An optional parent must be a native QWidget. Call it on the host thread. Run this from FontLab's scripting surface with your application's source path: from pythonqtside import run_app app_handle = run_app ( "/path/to/my_app.py" ) # Inspect app_handle.reports and app_handle.identity_report for routing details. # Keep the handle while the window is in use; close it when finished. app_handle . close () close() disconnects tracked connections, stops owned work and schedules owned object cleanup; repeated calls are safe. Inspect cleanup_errors for cleanup failures. Objects returned by arbitrary APIs are borrowed, not automatically owned. Dynamic exec/eval source, importlib imports, namespace packages and application subclasses/settings are unsupported. Namespace routing and this implemented runner do not establish full unchanged-app compatibility. Full acceptance still requires real native windows, callbacks, responsiveness, cleanup and owned-font editing/undo/save/reopen across the required application corpus. Reuse FontLab's application and event loop. Do not load a second Qt runtime or start a nested standalone application loop in the host.

title: Install into FontLab

text: To work on a package, install its Git checkout in editable mode into FontLab's per-user Python environment. When that folder is the site-packages of a virtual environment (for example a link into FontLab 9/.venv ), point --python at that environment's interpreter; --link-mode=copy copies files from uv's cache instead of linking them: FL_PY = " $HOME /Library/Application Support/FontLab/FontLab 9/.venv/bin/python" uv pip install --python " $FL_PY " --link-mode = copy -e path/to/fontlab-glyport uv pip install --python " $FL_PY " --link-mode = copy -e path/to/fontlab-fontport Repeat for each checkout you develop (Echopy, Fly, Fontlabapp, Grablab, Remopy, Aidus Code, Glyport, Fontport). Source edits are live in FontLab once the package's modules are reloaded. Restart FontLab, or remove the package's modules from sys.modules , to load a new version: FontLab keeps imported modules between script runs. Packages with compiled extensions must match FontLab's architecture (arm64 on Apple silicon). Install packages that run outside FontLab (Remopy, the documentation tools, TypeRig's core) into an ordinary environment with uv pip install PATH_TO_WHEEL . Private repositories require authenticated GitHub access; keep credentials in your GitHub tooling, never in scripts or URLs.
title: Editable install from a checkout

text: Every API page is generated without running FontLab: fontlab , fontgate , fontpr and PythonQt come from Echopy's captures of the live host (242,654 captured identities, each one documented). Modules that exist only while a Glyphs script runs ( GlyphsApp , vanilla , AppKit , Cocoa , Foundation , objc ), FontLab's menus and panels ( fontlabapp_shim ) and the Aidus tools ( aidus_code_tools ) come from Echopy shims generated from the providers FontLab scripts actually receive. The packages above are read from their source, never imported, so code that needs FontLab still documents completely. The build fails when any package renders no members or no documentation.
title: How this reference is built

text: Aidus Code adds an AI chat dock to FontLab 9. Ask about the current glyph, inspect fonts and metrics, change spacing, or have the agent write and run FontLab Python. Responses stream into the dock. The FontLab plugin runs in FontLab's Python 3.11. The AI "brain" runs in a separate Python 3.13+ process, so no AI libraries go into FontLab. The AI provider you configure receives your prompts and the tool results the agent uses. This page describes Aidus Code v0.2.1.
title: Aidus Code

text: Install the host package into a dedicated folder (Python 3.11): uv pip install --python 3 .11 --target ~/.local/share/fontlab-aidus/host PATH_TO_AIDUS_WHEEL Create the brain environment (Python 3.13+) with the brain extra and Remopy: uv venv --python 3 .13 ~/.local/share/fontlab-aidus/brain uv pip install --python ~/.local/share/fontlab-aidus/brain/bin/python \ 'PATH_TO_AIDUS_WHEEL[brain]' PATH_TO_REMOPY_WHEEL Install the Scripts-menu entries and check the setup: PYTHONPATH = ~/.local/share/fontlab-aidus/host python3 -m fontlab_aidus_code.install install PYTHONPATH = ~/.local/share/fontlab-aidus/host python3 -m fontlab_aidus_code.install check The installer records the files it owns. Reinstalling or uninstalling keeps your own files. An install stops before changing anything when a script it would replace was modified, is not its own or is a symlink. Configure the brain Python path and your AI provider keys as described in the package's configuration guide.
title: Install

text: In FontLab, open the Aidus Code entry in the Scripts menu. Try: "What are the sidebearings of the current glyph?" or "Set the right sidebearing of all selected glyphs to 50."
title: Quick start

text: The agent's FontLab tools are also callable from Python inside FontLab, through the Aidus tools reference : # Inside FontLab, with fontlab-aidus-code installed from fontlab_echopy import aidus_code_tools print ( aidus_code_tools . get_current_glyph_info ())
title: Programmatic tools

text: Use a disposable font for your first editing experiments: the agent can change and run code on the open font. Prompts and tool results go to your configured AI provider. Reference: fontlab_aidus_code . Aidus Code is proprietary (© Fontlab Ltd); only its API documentation is published here.
title: Limits

text: Echopy gives FontLab's native API ( fontlab , fontgate , fontpr , PythonQt ) a readable Python source form: classes, signatures, types and documentation that editors, type checkers and this site can read. At run time it hands you the original native objects, so nothing changes in behaviour. This page describes Echopy v0.2.3.
title: Echopy

text: Install the fontlab-echopy wheel into FontLab's Python folder (see Install into FontLab ). Both import names, echopy and fontlab_echopy , refer to the same modules.
title: Install

text: # Inside FontLab from echopy import fontlab as fl , fontgate as fg , fontpr node = fl . flNode ( 12 , 34 ) # the original native flNode assert fl . flNode is __import__ ( "fontlab" ) . flNode Outside FontLab the same imports load the declarations for documentation and type checking; calling a native function or constructing a native class raises NativeUnavailable .
title: Quick start

text: Inspect a declaration without FontLab: import inspect from echopy import fontlab as fl print ( inspect . signature ( fl . flNode . __init__ )) Static shims describe modules that exist only at run time, for example the GlyphsApp module Glyport builds for each Glyphs script: from fontlab_echopy import GlyphsApp # declarations only; see GlyphsApp reference
title: Examples

text: Small .py facades bind native symbols; full declarations live in .pyi sidecars, which keeps imports inside FontLab's five-second script deadline. Unknown native signatures stay explicit as *args, **kwargs ; PySide2 reference signatures are labelled as upstream and may differ from PythonQt. fontlabpr is absent from FontLab 9.0.9780 and documented as absent. Reference: fontlab_echopy , and the native fontlab , fontgate , fontpr and PythonQt pages.
title: How it works and limits

text: Fly gives the FontLab Python ecosystem nine short, lazy import aliases. Each alias is the exact original module object, not a copy or wrapper. Alias Module fl echopy.fontlab fg echopy.fontgate pr echopy.fontpr qt PythonQt tr typerig ap fontlabapp qs pythonqtside gp fontlab_glyport fp fontlab_fontport
title: fly

text: Install fontlab-fly with its target packages (Echopy, TypeRig, Fontlabapp, Pythonqtside, Glyport, Fontport) into FontLab's Python folder; see Install into FontLab .
title: Install

text: # Inside FontLab from fly import fl , fg , qt , gp , fp font = fl . CurrentFont () # same function as fontlab.CurrentFont import fly.gp , fontlab_glyport assert fly . gp is fontlab_glyport
title: Quick start

text: Child imports route to the canonical package: from fly.fp.pens import FontGatePointPen # same object as fontlab_fontport.pens from fly.tr.core.objects.point import Point
title: Examples

text: Importing fly loads none of its targets; each alias loads on first access. qt needs FontLab's native PythonQt; outside FontLab it raises a clear ModuleNotFoundError . Missing target packages raise the same way. Reference: fly .
title: Behaviour and limits

text: Fontlabapp is the Python layer for FontLab's application surface: menus and actions, panels, preferences, versions and paths, Glyph and Preview windows, drawing overlays, and docks, dialogs and widgets you create yourself. This page describes Fontlabapp v0.2.4.
title: fontlabapp

text: Install fontlab-fontlabapp into FontLab's Python folder; see Install into FontLab . Its utilities import outside FontLab without loading native modules or creating preference files.
title: Install

text: # Inside FontLab from fontlabapp import Application app = Application ( with_ui = True , with_preflib = False ) print ( app . versions . app_version ) with app . control as fl : print ( fl . fonts ()) fl . panel ( "preview" ) . show () fl . preview . set_text ( "Hamburgefonts" ) . set_font_size ( 48 )
title: Quick start

text: Draw on the Glyph window without changing the font. The overlay is removed when the context exits: from PythonQt import QtGui with app . control as fl : glyph_window = fl . glyph_window () # raises if no Glyph window is open def paint ( painter ): painter . setPen ( QtGui . QColor ( "#008000" )) painter . drawLine ( 30 , 30 , 100 , 100 ) with glyph_window . draw ( paint , coordinates = "canvas" ) as overlay : overlay . raise_if_failed () Create your own panel, modeless dialog or tool widget: def build ( widget ): layout = QtGui . QVBoxLayout ( widget ) layout . addWidget ( QtGui . QLabel ( "My tool" , widget )) with app . control as fl : panel = fl . create_panel ( "My panel" , build , area = "right" ) panel . close () The fontlabapp_shim reference lists FontLab's menus, actions and panels as Python names (788 of 788 resolve in FontLab 9).
title: Examples

text: fontlabapp.fontui provides ready-made Qt tools that work on an explicit font model (ufoLib2, defcon, or live FontParts objects from Fontport ). Install the extra that matches the tools you need: Extra Adds fontlab-fontlabapp[fontui] font_browser , glyph_browser , glyph_preview fontlab-fontlabapp[fontsequence] glyph_sequence fontlab-fontlabapp[fontedit] font_info_editor , groups_editor , kerning_editor , features_editor , designspace_panel , transform_editor , batch_panel Each function returns a handle. Keep a reference to it, show its .widget and call .close() when you are done. The browsers, preview, sequence and the info, groups, kerning and features editors also have .refresh() for edits made elsewhere; batch_panel , transform_editor and designspace_panel do not: # Inside FontLab, with the fontui extra and ufoLib2 installed from ufoLib2 import Font from fontlabapp.fontui import font_browser font = Font () # a detached demonstration model font . info . familyName = "Browser demonstration" glyph = font . newGlyph ( "A" ) glyph . width = 600 pen = glyph . getPen () pen . moveTo (( 50 , 0 )); pen . lineTo (( 300 , 700 )); pen . lineTo (( 550 , 0 )); pen . closePath () browser = font_browser ([ font ]) # keep this handle alive browser . widget . resize ( 850 , 1000 ) browser . widget . show () # ... later: browser . close () Editors stage changes and apply them in one validated batch; a model without a batch apply opens read-only. The font information editor also offers the structured fields OS/2 weight and width class, Panose (ten integers) and horizontal and vertical stem snaps; it labels them "key master" because Fontport writes them to the current key master only. Name records are not offered. While a script has unfinished point edits on a font, the controls that follow FontLab changes skip that font's reload rather than discard the edits, and show "A font has unfinished script edits; its view updates when the script finishes." The view updates on the next change after the script completes. batch_panel runs work in a separate Python 3.11+ process so FontLab stays responsive.
title: FontUI: font and glyph browsers and editors

text: Application(with_preflib=False) inspects the application without opening or saving the preference library. Native wrappers may be recreated on each access: compare fonts by native id, not with is . Created panels, dialogs and widgets own only themselves; close them when done. Reference: fontlabapp , FontLab menus and panels .
title: Limits

text: Fontport connects FontLab 9 to the Python font libraries most tools are built on: FontParts, fontTools and fontPens pens, and ufoLib2. It provides point pens over native FontGate glyphs, detached FontParts and UFO snapshots, and live FontParts objects bound to an open FontLab document.
title: Fontport

text: Install fontlab-fontport with fontTools, fontPens, FontParts and ufoLib2 into FontLab's Python folder; see Install into FontLab . Importing the package outside FontLab is safe; native access loads on demand.
title: Install

text: Draw into a native glyph with a fontTools pen: # Inside FontLab, with a glyph you own from fontlab_fontport.pens import FontGatePointPen from fontTools.pens.pointPen import SegmentToPointPen pen = SegmentToPointPen ( FontGatePointPen ( glyph )) pen . moveTo (( 0 , 0 )) pen . lineTo (( 200 , 0 )) pen . lineTo (( 100 , 300 )) pen . closePath ()
title: Quick start

text: Edit a detached FontParts copy, then write it back explicitly: from fontlab_fontport.transfer import to_fontparts , write_glyph snapshot = to_fontparts ( native_glyph ) # a real fontshell RGlyph snapshot . width = 600 write_glyph ( snapshot , target_glyph ) # explicit destination Bind live FontParts objects to an open FontLab document: from fontlab_fontport.host import NativeFontBackend from fontlab_fontport.live import RFont font = RFont ( NativeFontBackend ( font_id )) # font_id: the document's FontLab id font [ "A" ] . width = 600 # updates the FontLab glyph font . close () # detaches; the document stays open Stage font information and apply it in one validated batch: font . info . apply ({ "familyName" : "My Family" , "ascender" : 810.5 }, undo_name = "Edit font information" )
title: Examples

text: Undo: an edit through the live binding is undone by the first Edit > Undo. FontLab records one extra, empty Undo row with it (exact one-row Undo is the unsupported capability glyph.exactSingleUndo ; information batches likewise report info.exactSingleUndo ). Font information: metrics ( ascender , descender , capHeight , xHeight , italicAngle ), styleName and note are written to the current key master only; family name, version fields, copyright and units per em are stored on the font. Supported fields: familyName , styleName , unitsPerEm , ascender , descender , capHeight , xHeight , italicAngle , versionMajor , versionMinor , note and copyright . The structured fields openTypeOS2Panose , openTypeOS2WeightClass , openTypeOS2WidthClass , postscriptStemSnapH and postscriptStemSnapV are also written to the key master only. OpenType name records are refused, since FontLab does not persist them through this route. Default and strict modes: the v1.0.0 editing contract is the default. Stricter guarantees are opt-in: require_single_undo=True on font.info.apply and require_persistence=True on group and save operations refuse instead of accepting the extra Undo row or a legacy group mode. Named refusals: layer create, delete and rename; glyph rename; guidelines and images; hinted outlines; fractional anchors and kerning; non-ASCII names for new glyphs and groups; multi-layer UFO import; world selection. Each raises UnsupportedCapability with its name before anything is written. font.capabilities() lists every capability with its evidence. Edits made in FontLab itself do not notify the binding: call font.refresh() and reacquire glyph and layer handles afterwards. FontParts coverage (FontParts 1.1.1 upstream tests, host-free backend run): 1,748 of 1,797 pass, 48 raise a named UnsupportedCapability , one is skipped upstream, none fail unclassified. These are not FontLab-native passes. An unexpected FontLab error during the final write can leave partial changes; develop on a copy of your font. Reference: fontlab_fontport . Licence: Apache 2.0.
title: Behaviour and limits (Fontport v1.0.2)

text: Glyport runs Glyphs scripts and plugins inside FontLab. It inspects and adapts the original source (including Glyphs 2 / Python 2 code), gives each run a live GlyphsApp model backed by the FontLab font, and translates Vanilla, AppKit and NIB/XIB interfaces to FontLab's Qt. Original files are never modified. This page describes Glyport v1.0.2.
title: Glyport

text: Install fontlab-glyport into FontLab's Python folder; see Install into FontLab . Its inspection API also works outside FontLab.
title: Install

text: Assess a script without running it: from fontlab_glyport import inspect_source assessment = inspect_source ( "OriginalScript.py" ) print ( assessment . required_capabilities ) Run a Glyphs script inside FontLab: # Inside FontLab from fontlab_glyport import run_script handle = run_script ( "OriginalScript.py" ) # profile chosen from the source print ( handle . state , handle . receipt ) handle . close ()
title: Quick start

text: Install a plugin bundle and remove it again: from fontlab_glyport import install_plugin plugin = install_plugin ( "MyReporter.glyphsReporter" ) # ... the reporter now draws in the Glyph window ... plugin . unload () # removes every registration Adapt Glyphs 2 source into an owned cache, keeping a map back to original lines: from fontlab_glyport import adapt_source adapted = adapt_source ( "OldScript.py" , profile = "glyphs2" , cache_dir = ".glyport-cache" ) code = adapted . compile () # compiles; does not execute print ( adapted . translate ( 1 , 1 )) # generated position -> original position
title: Examples

text: The GlyphsApp module for each run: Glyphs , the GS* model classes, callback events and dialogs ( GlyphsApp reference ). The seven Glyphs SDK plugin classes ( GeneralPlugin , FilterWithoutDialog , FilterWithDialog , ReporterPlugin , PalettePlugin , SelectTool , FileFormatPlugin ), registered as real FontLab menu actions, windows, export items and Glyph-window painters. Vanilla controls and dialogs, Qt-backed AppKit classes, NSBezierPath drawing and NIB/XIB interface loading ( vanilla , AppKit ).
title: What is supported

text: Compatibility is partial and still being extended; each run records a receipt with the outcome, and unsupported features raise UnsupportedCapability at the script line instead of failing silently. FontLab host limits block SelectTool and drawing before FontLab's own glyph layer; plugins that need them are reported as blocked. Bundles that ship only compiled macOS code cannot run. Creating glyphs makes FontLab rebuild auto-layer composites. Glyport restores existing composites afterwards and refuses with a named reason when it cannot. A FontLab defect can still drop component locks and attaching anchors on composites it rebuilds. Edits on auto layers (outlines, anchors, guides, hints, width, background) are refused before anything changes: telling FontLab about an auto-layer edit makes it rebuild every auto layer in the font. Test with a copy of your font: scripts can change the font they run on. See the Glyphs compatibility guide . Reference: fontlab_glyport .
title: Limits

text: Grablab captures FontLab's interface for documentation and tests: panels, menus, Glyph and Font windows, screens and widgets, as PNG, SVG or PDF with title and description metadata.
title: grablab

text: Install fontlab-grablab together with fontlab-fontlabapp into FontLab's Python folder; see Install into FontLab . Importing grablab is host-free; capturing needs FontLab.
title: Install

text: # Inside FontLab from grablab import Grab capture = Grab ( grab_canvas = False , grab_screens = False ) capture . newGrab () paths = capture . grabPanel ( "elements" ) print ( paths )
title: Quick start

text: Capture a widget, including a Fontlabapp drawing overlay, as SVG and PNG: from pathlib import Path from fontlabapp import Application from grablab import Grab app = Application () folder = Path . home () / "Desktop" / "captures" folder . mkdir ( exist_ok = True ) grab = Grab ( application = app , folder_base = folder ) with app . control as fl : grab . getWidgetSVG ( fl . preview . widget , folder / "preview.svg" )
title: Examples

text: Capture temporarily changes OpenGL, outline-thickness and pixel-rendering preferences and restores them afterwards, even on failure. OpenGL canvases have Qt framebuffer limits; the non-OpenGL Glyph view and Preview paths are verified. Reference: grablab .
title: Limits

text: Pythonqtside lets code written for PySide2 ( QtCore , QtGui , QtWidgets , …) run on FontLab's built-in PythonQt. It routes each PySide2 name to the native class and adapts the differences that matter in practice: keyword arguments, property getters, overloads and protected event handlers. It never loads a second Qt binding or creates a QApplication .
title: pythonqtside

text: Install pythonqtside (it depends on Echopy) into FontLab's Python folder; see Install into FontLab .
title: Install

text: # Inside FontLab from pythonqtside import QtCore , QtGui , QtWidgets widget = QtWidgets . QWidget () # the original native QWidget layout = QtWidgets . QVBoxLayout ( widget ) layout . addWidget ( QtWidgets . QLabel ( "Hello from PySide2-style code" )) widget . show ()
title: Quick start

text: Port an existing PySide2 tool by changing only its import: # from PySide2 import QtCore, QtWidgets from pythonqtside import QtCore , QtWidgets Available namespaces: QtCore , QtGui , QtWidgets , QtNetwork , QtOpenGL , QtSvg , QtUiTools , QtXmlPatterns and the combined Qt .
title: Examples

text: Use FontLab's running application; do not call QApplication.exec() . Names alone do not guarantee identical behaviour: enum conversion, ownership and some overloads differ from PySide2. See the PySide2 guide . Qt 6 / PySide6 is not supported (FontLab 9 uses Qt 5). Reference: pythonqtside .
title: Limits

text: Remopy controls a running FontLab 9 from another Python process through FontLab's native MCP server: run code, read values, open and save fonts and call any FontLab tool. It also launches FontLab and submits scripts on macOS.
title: Remopy

text: Install the fontlab-remopy wheel into your ordinary Python 3.11+ environment (not into FontLab). Enable FontLab's MCP server once: fontlab-remopy launch fontlab-remopy --timeout 15 setup
title: Install

text: from fontlab_remopy import FontLab with FontLab () as fl : print ( fl . fonts ()) answer = fl . eval ( "value + 2" , value = 40 ) # 42 done = fl . run ( "print(message); result = {'ok': True}" , message = "Hello" ) print ( done . value , done . stdout )
title: Quick start

text: Write a function locally and run it inside FontLab: with FontLab () as fl : @fl . python def metrics ( name : str ): import fontpr return fontpr . get_glyph_metrics ( glyph_name = name ) print ( metrics ( "A" )) # with an open font containing A Run a script file and call tools from the command line: fontlab-remopy tools fontlab-remopy execute example.flpy fontlab-remopy call list_fonts Use AsyncFontLab with async with and await in asynchronous programs.
title: Examples

text: Values travel as JSON; native objects cannot be returned directly. FontLab's fixed five-second script deadline applies. A timeout leaves the outcome unknown, so mutating calls are never retried automatically. Launch and file association are macOS only; MCP works wherever FontLab's bridge executable is available. Reference: fontlab_remopy . Remopy is proprietary (© Fontlab Ltd); only its API documentation is published here.
title: Limits

text: TypeRig is Vassil Kateliev's font-development library: outline objects, points and contours, interpolation and adaptive scaling, and proxies over FontLab's objects. This package distributes the complete library; TypeRig's GUI scripts, panels and toolbars stay in kateliev/TypeRig .
title: typerig

text: python -m pip install typerig The core needs no FontLab. Install it into FontLab's Python folder as well to use the FontLab proxies; see Install into FontLab .
title: Install

text: from typerig.core.objects.point import Point point = Point ( 10 , 20 ) + Point ( 2 , 3 ) print ( point . x , point . y ) # 12.0 23.0
title: Quick start

text: Inside FontLab, use the proxy layer on the current glyph: from typerig.proxy.fl.objects.glyph import eGlyph glyph = eGlyph () # wraps the current glyph print ( glyph . name , glyph . getBounds ())
title: Examples

text: Proxy modules need their host API (FontLab, or Glyphs for the Glyphs proxies). Licence: Mozilla Public License 2.0 (upstream TypeRig). Reference: typerig .

title: PythonQt.Qt.QAbstractAnimation

text: The class defines the functions for the functionality shared by all animations. By inheriting this class, you can create custom animations that plug into the rest of the animation framework. The progress of an animation is given by its current time ( currentLoopTime ()), which is measured in milliseconds from the start of the animation (0) to its end ( duration ()). The value is updated automatically while the animation is running. It can also be set directly with setCurrentTime (). At any point an animation is in one of three states: Running , Stopped , or Paused --as defined by the State enum. The current state can be changed by calling start (), stop (), pause (), or resume (). An animation will always reset its current time when it is started. If paused, it will continue with the same current time when resumed. When an animation is stopped, it cannot be resumed, but will keep its current time (until started again). QAbstractAnimation will emit stateChanged () whenever its state changes. An animation can loop any number of times by setting the loopCount property. When an animation's current time reaches its duration (), it will reset the current time and keep running. A loop count of 1 (the default value) means that the animation will run one time. Note that a duration of -1 means that the animation will run until stopped; the current time will increase indefinitely. When the current time equals duration () and the animation is in its final loop, the Stopped state is entered, and the finished () signal is emitted. QAbstractAnimation provides pure virtual functions used by subclasses to track the progress of the animation: duration () and updateCurrentTime (). The duration () function lets you report a duration for the animation (as discussed above). The animation framework calls updateCurrentTime () when current time has changed. By reimplementing this function, you can track the animation progress. Note that neither the interval between calls nor the number of calls to this function are defined; though, it will normally be 60 updates per second. By reimplementing updateState (), you can track the animation's state changes, which is particularly useful for animations that are not driven by time. Source: https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractanimation.html

title: PythonQt.Qt.QAbstractButton

text: This class implements an abstract button. Subclasses of this class handle user actions, and specify how the button is drawn. QAbstractButton provides support for both push buttons and checkable (toggle) buttons. Checkable buttons are implemented in the QRadioButton and QCheckBox classes. Push buttons are implemented in the QPushButton and QToolButton classes; these also provide toggle behavior if required. Any button can display a label containing text and an icon. setText () sets the text; setIcon () sets the icon. If a button is disabled, its label is changed to give the button a "disabled" appearance. If the button is a text button with a string containing an ampersand ('\&'), QAbstractButton automatically creates a shortcut key. For example: QPushButton *button = new QPushButton(tr("Ro&ck && Roll"), this); The Alt+C shortcut is assigned to the button, i.e., when the user presses Alt+C the button will call animateClick (). See the QShortcut documentation for details. To display an actual ampersand, use '\&\&'. You can also set a custom shortcut key using the setShortcut () function. This is useful mostly for buttons that do not have any text, and therefore can't have any automatic shortcut. button->setIcon(QIcon(":/images/print.png")); button->setShortcut(tr("Alt+F7")); All the buttons provided by Qt ( QPushButton , QToolButton , QCheckBox , and QRadioButton ) can display both text and icons . A button can be made the default button in a dialog by means of QPushButton::setDefault () and QPushButton::setAutoDefault (). QAbstractButton provides most of the states used for buttons: isDown () indicates whether the button is pressed down. isChecked () indicates whether the button is checked . Only checkable buttons can be checked and unchecked (see below). isEnabled () indicates whether the button can be pressed by the user. Note: As opposed to other widgets, buttons derived from QAbstractButton accept mouse and context menu events when disabled. - setAutoRepeat () sets whether the button will auto-repeat if the user holds it down. autoRepeatDelay and autoRepeatInterval define how auto-repetition is done. - setCheckable () sets whether the button is a toggle button or not. The difference between isDown () and isChecked () is as follows. When the user clicks a toggle button to check it, the button is first pressed then released into the checked state. When the user clicks it again (to uncheck it), the button moves first to the pressed state, then to the unchecked state ( isChecked () and isDown () are both false). QAbstractButton provides four signals: pressed () is emitted when the left mouse button is pressed while the mouse cursor is inside the button. released () is emitted when the left mouse button is released. clicked () is emitted when the button is first pressed and then released, when the shortcut key is typed, or when click () or animateClick () is called. toggled () is emitted when the state of a toggle button changes. To subclass QAbstractButton, you must reimplement at least paintEvent () to draw the button's outline and its text or pixmap. It is generally advisable to reimplement sizeHint () as well, and sometimes hitButton () (to determine whether a button press is within the button). For buttons with more than two states (like tri-state buttons), you will also have to reimplement checkStateSet () and nextCheckState (). Source: https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractbutton.html

title: PythonQt.Qt.QAbstractItemDelegate

text: A QAbstractItemDelegate provides the interface and common functionality for delegates in the model/view architecture. Delegates display individual items in views, and handle the editing of model data. The QAbstractItemDelegate class is one of the Model/View Classes and is part of Qt's model/view framework . To render an item in a custom way, you must implement paint () and sizeHint (). The QStyledItemDelegate class provides default implementations for these functions; if you do not need custom rendering, subclass that class instead. We give an example of drawing a progress bar in items; in our case for a package management program. We create the WidgetDelegate class, which inherits from QStyledItemDelegate . We do the drawing in the paint () function: void WidgetDelegate::paint(QPainter *painter, const QStyleOptionViewItem &option, const QModelIndex &index) const { if (index.column() == 1) { int progress = index.data().toInt(); QStyleOptionProgressBar progressBarOption; progressBarOption.rect = option.rect; progressBarOption.minimum = 0; progressBarOption.maximum = 100; progressBarOption.progress = progress; progressBarOption.text = QString::number(progress) + "%"; progressBarOption.textVisible = true; QApplication::style()->drawControl(QStyle::CE_ProgressBar, &progressBarOption, painter); } else QStyledItemDelegate::paint(painter, option, index); Notice that we use a QStyleOptionProgressBar and initialize its members. We can then use the current QStyle to draw it. To provide custom editing, there are two approaches that can be used. The first approach is to create an editor widget and display it directly on top of the item. To do this you must reimplement createEditor () to provide an editor widget, setEditorData () to populate the editor with the data from the model, and setModelData () so that the delegate can update the model with data from the editor. The second approach is to handle user events directly by reimplementing editorEvent (). Source: https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemdelegate.html

title: PythonQt.Qt.QAbstractItemModel

text: The QAbstractItemModel class defines the standard interface that item models must use to be able to interoperate with other components in the model/view architecture. It is not supposed to be instantiated directly. Instead, you should subclass it to create new models. The QAbstractItemModel class is one of the Model/View Classes and is part of Qt's model/view framework . It can be used as the underlying data model for the item view elements in QML or the item view classes in the Qt Widgets module. If you need a model to use with an item view such as QML's List View element or the C++ widgets QListView or QTableView , you should consider subclassing QAbstractListModel or QAbstractTableModel instead of this class. The underlying data model is exposed to views and delegates as a hierarchy of tables. If you do not make use of the hierarchy, then the model is a simple table of rows and columns. Each item has a unique index specified by a QModelIndex . Every item of data that can be accessed via a model has an associated model index. You can obtain this model index using the index () function. Each index may have a sibling () index; child items have a parent () index. Each item has a number of data elements associated with it and they can be retrieved by specifying a role (see Qt::ItemDataRole ) to the model's data () function. Data for all available roles can be obtained at the same time using the itemData () function. Data for each role is set using a particular Qt::ItemDataRole . Data for individual roles are set individually with setData (), or they can be set for all roles with setItemData (). Items can be queried with flags () (see Qt::ItemFlag ) to see if they can be selected, dragged, or manipulated in other ways. If an item has child objects, hasChildren () returns true for the corresponding index. The model has a rowCount () and a columnCount () for each level of the hierarchy. Rows and columns can be inserted and removed with insertRows (), insertColumns (), removeRows (), and removeColumns (). The model emits signals to indicate changes. For example, dataChanged () is emitted whenever items of data made available by the model are changed. Changes to the headers supplied by the model cause headerDataChanged () to be emitted. If the structure of the underlying data changes, the model can emit layoutChanged () to indicate to any attached views that they should redisplay any items shown, taking the new structure into account. The items available through the model can be searched for particular data using the match () function. To sort the model, you can use sort ().
title: Detailed Description

text: Note: Some general guidelines for subclassing models are available in the Model Subclassing Reference . When subclassing QAbstractItemModel, at the very least you must implement index (), parent (), rowCount (), columnCount (), and data (). These functions are used in all read-only models, and form the basis of editable models. You can also reimplement hasChildren () to provide special behavior for models where the implementation of rowCount () is expensive. This makes it possible for models to restrict the amount of data requested by views, and can be used as a way to implement lazy population of model data. To enable editing in your model, you must also implement setData (), and reimplement flags () to ensure that ItemIsEditable is returned. You can also reimplement headerData () and setHeaderData () to control the way the headers for your model are presented. The dataChanged () and headerDataChanged () signals must be emitted explicitly when reimplementing the setData () and setHeaderData () functions, respectively. Custom models need to create model indexes for other components to use. To do this, call createIndex () with suitable row and column numbers for the item, and an identifier for it, either as a pointer or as an integer value. The combination of these values must be unique for each item. Custom models typically use these unique identifiers in other reimplemented functions to retrieve item data and access information about the item's parents and children. See the Simple Tree Model Example for more information about unique identifiers. It is not necessary to support every role defined in Qt::ItemDataRole . Depending on the type of data contained within a model, it may only be useful to implement the data () function to return valid information for some of the more common roles. Most models provide at least a textual representation of item data for the Qt::DisplayRole , and well-behaved models should also provide valid information for the Qt::ToolTipRole and Qt::WhatsThisRole . Supporting these roles enables models to be used with standard Qt views. However, for some models that handle highly-specialized data, it may be appropriate to provide data only for user-defined roles. Models that provide interfaces to resizable data structures can provide implementations of insertRows (), removeRows (), insertColumns (),and removeColumns (). When implementing these functions, it is important to notify any connected views about changes to the model's dimensions both before and after they occur: An insertRows () implementation must call beginInsertRows () before inserting new rows into the data structure, and endInsertRows () immediately afterwards . An insertColumns () implementation must call beginInsertColumns () before inserting new columns into the data structure, and endInsertColumns () immediately afterwards . A removeRows () implementation must call beginRemoveRows () before the rows are removed from the data structure, and endRemoveRows () immediately afterwards . A removeColumns () implementation must call beginRemoveColumns () before the columns are removed from the data structure, and endRemoveColumns () immediately afterwards . The private signals that these functions emit give attached components the chance to take action before any data becomes unavailable. The encapsulation of the insert and remove operations with these begin and end functions also enables the model to manage persistent model indexes correctly. If you want selections to be handled properly, you must ensure that you call these functions. If you insert or remove an item with children, you do not need to call these functions for the child items. In other words, the parent item will take care of its child items. To create models that populate incrementally, you can reimplement fetchMore () and canFetchMore (). If the reimplementation of fetchMore () adds rows to the model, beginInsertRows() and endInsertRows() must be called. Source: https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemmodel.html

title: PythonQt.Qt.QAbstractItemView

text: QAbstractItemView class is the base class for every standard view that uses a QAbstractItemModel . QAbstractItemView is an abstract class and cannot itself be instantiated. It provides a standard interface for interoperating with models through the signals and slots mechanism, enabling subclasses to be kept up-to-date with changes to their models. This class provides standard support for keyboard and mouse navigation, viewport scrolling, item editing, and selections. The keyboard navigation implements this functionality: Keys Functionality Arrow keys Changes the current item and selects it. Ctrl+Arrow keys Changes the current item but does not select it. Shift+Arrow keys Changes the current item and selects it. The previously selected item(s) is not deselected. Ctr+Space Toggles selection of the current item. Tab/Backtab Changes the current item to the next/previous item. Home/End Selects the first/last item in the model. Page up/Page down Scrolls the rows shown up/down by the number of visible rows in the view. Ctrl+A Selects all items in the model. Note that the above table assumes that the selection mode allows the operations. For instance, you cannot select items if the selection mode is QAbstractItemView::NoSelection . The QAbstractItemView class is one of the Model/View Classes and is part of Qt's model/view framework . The view classes that inherit QAbstractItemView only need to implement their own view-specific functionality, such as drawing items, returning the geometry of items, finding items, etc. QAbstractItemView provides common slots such as edit () and setCurrentIndex (). Many protected slots are also provided, including dataChanged (), rowsInserted (), rowsAboutToBeRemoved (), selectionChanged (), and currentChanged (). The root item is returned by rootIndex (), and the current item by currentIndex (). To make sure that an item is visible use scrollTo (). Some of QAbstractItemView's functions are concerned with scrolling, for example setHorizontalScrollMode () and setVerticalScrollMode (). To set the range of the scroll bars, you can, for example, reimplement the view's resizeEvent () function: void MyView::resizeEvent(QResizeEvent *event) { horizontalScrollBar()->setRange(0, realWidth - width()); ... } Note that the range is not updated until the widget is shown. Several other functions are concerned with selection control; for example setSelectionMode (), and setSelectionBehavior (). This class provides a default selection model to work with ( selectionModel ()), but this can be replaced by using setSelectionModel () with an instance of QItemSelectionModel . For complete control over the display and editing of items you can specify a delegate with setItemDelegate (). QAbstractItemView provides a lot of protected functions. Some are concerned with editing, for example, edit (), and commitData (), whilst others are keyboard and mouse event handlers. Note: If you inherit QAbstractItemView and intend to update the contents of the viewport, you should use viewport-> update () instead of update() as all painting operations take place on the viewport. Source: https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractitemview.html

title: PythonQt.Qt.QAbstractListModel

text: QAbstractListModel provides a standard interface for models that represent their data as a simple non-hierarchical sequence of items. It is not used directly, but must be subclassed. Since the model provides a more specialized interface than QAbstractItemModel , it is not suitable for use with tree views; you will need to subclass QAbstractItemModel if you want to provide a model for that purpose. If you need to use a number of list models to manage data, it may be more appropriate to subclass QAbstractTableModel instead. Simple models can be created by subclassing this class and implementing the minimum number of required functions. For example, we could implement a simple read-only QStringList -based model that provides a list of strings to a QListView widget. In such a case, we only need to implement the rowCount () function to return the number of items in the list, and the data () function to retrieve items from the list. Since the model represents a one-dimensional structure, the rowCount () function returns the total number of items in the model. The columnCount () function is implemented for interoperability with all kinds of views, but by default informs views that the model contains only one column.
title: Detailed Description

text: When subclassing QAbstractListModel, you must provide implementations of the rowCount () and data () functions. Well behaved models also provide a headerData () implementation. If your model is used within QML and requires roles other than the default ones provided by the roleNames () function, you must override it. For editable list models, you must also provide an implementation of setData (), and implement the flags () function so that it returns a value containing Qt::ItemIsEditable . Note that QAbstractListModel provides a default implementation of columnCount () that informs views that there is only a single column of items in this model. Models that provide interfaces to resizable list-like data structures can provide implementations of insertRows () and removeRows (). When implementing these functions, it is important to call the appropriate functions so that all connected views are aware of any changes: An insertRows () implementation must call beginInsertRows () before inserting new rows into the data structure, and it must call endInsertRows () immediately afterwards . A removeRows () implementation must call beginRemoveRows () before the rows are removed from the data structure, and it must call endRemoveRows () immediately afterwards . Note: Some general guidelines for subclassing models are available in the Model Subclassing Reference . Source: https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractlistmodel.html

title: PythonQt.Qt.QAbstractMessageHandler

text: QAbstractMessageHandler is an abstract base class that provides a callback interface for handling messages. For example, class QXmlQuery parses and runs an XQuery . When it detects a compile or runtime error, it generates an appropriate error message, but rather than output the message itself, it passes the message to the message () function of its QAbstractMessageHandler. See QXmlQuery::setMessageHandler (). You create a message handler by subclassing QAbstractMessageHandler and implementing handleMessage (). You then pass a pointer to an instance of your subclass to any classes that must generate messages. The messages are sent to the message handler via the message () function, which forwards them to your handleMessge(). A single instance of QAbstractMessageHandler can be called on to handle messages from multiple sources. Hence, the content of a message, which is the description parameter passed to message () and handleMessage (), must be interpreted in light of the context that required the message to be sent. That context is specified by the identifier and sourceLocation parameters to message () handleMessage (). Source: https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractmessagehandler.html

title: PythonQt.Qt.QAbstractProxyModel

text: This class defines the standard interface that proxy models must use to be able to interoperate correctly with other model/view components. It is not supposed to be instantiated directly. All standard proxy models are derived from the QAbstractProxyModel class. If you need to create a new proxy model class, it is usually better to subclass an existing class that provides the closest behavior to the one you want to provide. Proxy models that filter or sort items of data from a source model should be created by using or subclassing QSortFilterProxyModel . To subclass QAbstractProxyModel, you need to implement mapFromSource () and mapToSource (). The mapSelectionFromSource () and mapSelectionToSource () functions only need to be reimplemented if you need a behavior different from the default behavior. Note: If the source model is deleted or no source model is specified, the proxy model operates on a empty placeholder model. Source: https://doc.qt.io/archives/qt-5.15/qabstractproxymodel.html
